newsitem.title: INDIA: India says Australian wheat not contaminated.
newsitem.headline: India says Australian wheat not contaminated.

text.p: India's state-run State Trading Corp (STC) on Tuesday rejected a newspaper report that wheat imported from Australia may be contaminated.
The daily Financial Express said on Monday the Agriculture Ministry had warned that recent imports of Australian wheat "may be contaminated and the situation may well be alarming".
It said the ministry's plant quarantine division had reported evidence of "exotic weed seeds" in wheat samples taken at Indian ports.

It said authorities had decided to divert the wheat to southern India, where the grain is not grown, and to prevent it from reaching northern or western areas to prevent infection of India's own crop.
STC said in a statement that the newspaper "gives an erroneous impression that the imported wheat is infected".
It added, "This is far from the truth. The Australian wheat has one of the highest quality standards and has been permitted for distribution in India only after proper inspection and trading."
STC said the entire 1.4 million tonnes of Australian wheat that had already arrived had been fully tested by the Australian Wheat Board before shipment.
The wheat had been tested further by the Indian government and released for public distribution after being cleared by the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI), it said.

STC said the presence of weed in wheat from any source was not unusual, and Indian plant protection and quarantine authorities had taken precautionary measures, including pre-shipment inspection by Indian authorities at loading ports.
It did not indicate whether the shipments had been diverted to southern India.

In December, India authorised the STC to import two million tonnes of wheat to build stocks and check rising prices. STC officials said they had so far contracted to import 1.75 million tonnes, mainly from Australia, Argentina and Canada.
STC said the entire quantity had already arrived at the Indian ports.
Agriculture Ministry officials were unavailable for comment.
